opening: Over 100 million Americans have high blood pressure. This is concerning because high blood pressure can lead to cardiovascular disease, which is the leading cause of death worldwide. The easiest way to prevent this is to monitor your blood pressure and take steps to reduce it. The first question many people ask is, how often should you take your blood pressure? You want to monitor your blood pressure, but you also want accurate measurements. This guide will help you understand the ins and outs of taking your blood pressure. How Often Should You Take Your Blood Pressure The frequency that you test your blood pressure will depend on your health history. At a minimum, you should have your blood pressure
continuation: taken at least once a year during an annual checkup with your health care provider. Unless your blood pressure is high or your doctor tells you otherwise, you may not need to monitor your blood pressure more frequently than this. Some people, however, need to take their blood pressure more frequently, which requires the use of a blood pressure monitor at home. People with high blood pressure, heart disease or diabetes will want to measure their blood pressure more regularly. People who have undergone a recent change in their lifestyle, including losing weight or taking a new medication, will want to measure their blood pressure more frequently. How Often Should You Take Your Blood Pressure If your blood pressure is high or your lifestyle changes, you should check your blood pressure twice a day to monitor it more closely. If you check your blood pressure too frequently, it can cause anxiety, which can raise your blood pressure. How Often Should You Take Your Blood Pressure If you have low blood pressure, checking it too frequently can cause anxiety, which can raise your blood pressure. When Should You Take Your Blood Pressure? Generally, blood pressure is lowest in the morning just after you wake up. It will then rise during the day and peak in the late afternoon. As a result, taking your blood pressure at any time during the day will not give you an accurate picture of your blood pressure, and it should not be used to diagnose high blood pressure. Ideally, you should take your blood pressure sitting down after you have had a few minutes to rest. You should not take your blood pressure right after exercising or right before bed. What Causes High Blood Pressure? The cause of high blood pressure is often unknown and goes by the name “essential hypertension.” In about 5 to 10 percent of cases, it can be traced to a direct cause. This is known as secondary hypertension. For most people, high blood pressure can be traced to factors such as obesity, smoking, excessive alcohol use, stress, lack of exercise and poor diet. The right blood pressure monitor can help you take control of your blood pressure.

opening: Have you been brushing your teeth the right way? There are many bad tooth brushing habits that you might have developed over the years without even knowing. Next time you brush your teeth, take a moment and think about how you’re brushing. Here are some common mistakes: Rushing the brush: Not brushing long enough You might be rushing your brush without even realizing it. Brushing for too short of a time means your teeth don’t get as clean as they should be. You should be brushing your teeth for at least 2 minutes, but 3 is even better. You might want to set a timer to see how long you’re spending brushing your teeth. Many electric toothbrushes also shut off

Put pressure on your teeth with the brush or brush too hard: Apply pressure on your teeth with your toothbrush Electric toothbrushes apply the pressure for you, so you don’t have to worry about it with that. Manual toothbrushes need more pressure to clean well, but it’s not that much pressure. Putting too much pressure on your teeth with a manual toothbrush can damage your gums, and the enamel of your teeth. Brushing too hard with your manual toothbrush will have the same effect. Your gums will also hurt after a while if you brush too hard. The bristles should actually bend when you touch them to your teeth. Brushing too hard will also wear down the bristles faster, so you’ll need to replace your toothbrush more often. Using the wrong kind of toothbrush: using a hard bristle toothbrush It might seem like a toothbrush with harder bristles would clean your teeth better, but you’d be wrong. These toothbrushes are harder on your teeth and gums, so don’t use them. If you have sensitive teeth or gums, a soft-bristled toothbrush is your best option. Brushing with a toothbrush that’s too small: get a toothbrush that fits your mouth You want a toothbrush with a handle that you can easily hold and a toothbrush head that fits in your mouth comfortably. Toothbrush heads come in many sizes, but you want one that fits your mouth well. If your toothbrush head is too small or too big, it can make it harder to brush your teeth the way you should. Inadequate brushing of the back teeth: brush the backs and fronts of all your teeth A common mistake is to brush only the fronts of your teeth. These areas are especially prone to plaque build-up.

opening: The sun is rising on a new era for renewable energy in Gainesville, Fla. Starting this month, residents and business owners with solar panels connected to the power grid will get a monthly check from their city-owned electric utility, the result of a first-in-the-nation policy called a feed-in tariff. The new policy essentially turns privately owned rooftop solar panels into micro power generators for the utility. The city will pay up to 32 cents per kilowatt-hour for power they generate over the next 20 years, delivering their owners about a 5 percent profit over the equipment's lifespan. Feed-in tariffs like this have long been the primary tool for financing renewable energy projects in Europe, and they are a reason Spain
continuation:
, Germany and Portugal are leaders in the field, with renewable electricity that accounts for nearly a quarter of total power output.

Many renewable energy advocates now believe it's time for feed-in tariffs to come to the United States. The idea for such a policy in Gainesville initially came from voter John Tully, who owns a solar install company called Blue Planet Solar and was also a city commissioner in Gainesville. The plan was conceived in 2009, when Tully organized a group to draft a proposal and lobby city council members. "One of the big hurdles in the U.S. is getting access to financing," Tully says. "If you look at the rest of the world, you see feed-in tariffs are a proven tool that works."

The Gainesville City Commission approved the policy in April 2009, and it went into effect in April 2010. Some environmental groups, such as the Gainesville Green Energy Coalition, had their reservations, but ultimately supported the policy in light of the fact that Gainesville does not allow net metering, the traditional way utilities pay for solar power and other renewable energy. "The goal is to get more solar installed, and frankly, if we can get it done through the Gainesville program, we're happy," says Nancy Lowery, the group's executive director. The first round of applications will be judged by the end of the month, according to Gainesville Regional Utilities Director Thomas Wilkins, and the checks will start going out in January. Like many feed-in tariff programs, Gainesville's structure is a bit complex. The tariff is paid for each kilowatt-hour of electricity generated, and the exact price depends on two factors: the size of the system and when it is installed. The smaller the system, the more the city will pay for each kilowatt-hour (up to 32 cents per kilowatt-hour for systems under 10 kilowatts), and the longer a system takes to get installed, the lower the feed-in tariff rate (it decreases by 1 percent every three months). Incentives also exist to install solar panels on schools, churches and community centers, and systems with battery storage will be paid at a higher rate. Applications for the second round of approvals will be open through August 2011, after which the tariff will drop to 23 cents per kilowatt-hour (for under-10-kilowatt systems).

The system is set up to turn a profit for the city. "Our goal is to break even," Wilkins says. "If we give out too much, or too little, we'll lose money." In the first year, Wilkins says, the system's finances will be closely monitored to ensure it does not end up costing more than it brings in. Because it is a fixed price, there is no telling how much the city will pay out over the life of the program. "One of the things that we're still trying to analyze is, how does this scale?" he says. "If this thing goes huge, then maybe the price isn't right."
